title: Laws of Motion — Class 12 NIOS Physics
subject: Physics

slides.title: Laws of Motion
bullets: Class 12 — NIOS Physics
Chapter 3
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. Today we move from kinematics to dynamics — the why of motion. Newton's three laws are the cornerstone of classical mechanics.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: State and apply Newton's three laws.
Use F = ma and F = dp/dt for force / acceleration / momentum problems.
Apply momentum conservation to recoil and collisions.
Apply f_s ≤ μ_s N and f_k = μ_k N to friction problems.
Solve inclined-plane and connected-body problems.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each; ask which feels least comfortable.

slides.title: Force and inertia
bullets: Force = vector push or pull.
SI unit: newton (N) = kg·m/s².
Inertia = resistance to change in motion. Mass measures inertia.
Three kinds: rest, motion, direction.
More mass → more inertia.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the bus-jolt example to link inertia of rest / motion to everyday observation.

slides.title: Newton's first law
bullets: Body at rest stays at rest; body in uniform motion stays in uniform motion — unless a net force acts.
Defines what a force is: anything that changes motion.
Holds in inertial frames only.
Friction explains why everyday objects slow down.
Also called the law of inertia.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress that 'no force' is the natural state, not 'rest'. Galileo's insight.

slides.title: Newton's second law
bullets: F_net = dp/dt; for constant mass: F = ma.
1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s² (definition).
Doubling F doubles a (for fixed m).
Free-body diagram is always step 1.
Linear momentum p = mv (vector, kg·m/s).
slides.speaker_notes: Demo: pull a cart with a spring scale, measure F, time the acceleration. Verify F = ma.

slides.title: Worked: impulse-momentum
bullets: Ball 0.1 kg, 20 m/s → caught in 0.05 s.
Impulse magnitude = 2 N·s.
Average force = Δp/Δt = 2/0.05 = 40 N.
Stretching catch (longer Δt) reduces peak force.
slides.speaker_notes: Tie to airbag / catching a fast cricket ball.

slides.title: Newton's third law
bullets: Action = −Reaction.
Equal magnitude, opposite direction.
Act on DIFFERENT bodies — they don't cancel.
Examples: walking, recoil, rocket, swimming.
Pairs are of the same kind (both contact, both gravity, etc.).
slides.speaker_notes: Address the horse–cart 'paradox': forces on horse vs forces on cart are different — analyse separately.

slides.title: Conservation of linear momentum
bullets: In an isolated system (no external net force), total p is constant.
Follows from Newton's third law.
Holds in any collision (elastic or inelastic).
Recoil: m_g v_g = m_b v_b.
Stick collision: m₁ u₁ + m₂ u₂ = (m₁ + m₂) v.
slides.speaker_notes: Demo with skateboards or low-friction carts before the slide.

slides.title: Worked: gun recoil
bullets: Gun 2 kg, bullet 0.005 kg @ 500 m/s.
Initial momentum = 0 (system at rest).
Gun recoils at 1.25 m/s opposite the bullet.
Heavier gun → smaller recoil (good design).
slides.speaker_notes: After the example, ask: 'Why are heavier rifles preferred for high-speed bullets?' (less recoil).

slides.title: Friction
bullets: Static: f_s ≤ μ_s N (adjusts to balance applied force).
Kinetic: f_k = μ_k N (constant while sliding).
μ_k < μ_s for the same surfaces.
Independent of contact area.
Useful (walking, braking) AND harmful (energy loss, wear).
slides.speaker_notes: Tilt the inclined-plane demo until the block slips; that angle is the angle of repose.

slides.title: Worked: angle of repose
bullets: Block on incline; just on the verge of sliding.
Along incline: mg sin θ_r = μ_s mg cos θ_r.
tan θ_r = μ_s.
Measure θ_r → get μ_s directly.
A simple, robust experimental method.
slides.speaker_notes: Try it with the wooden block. If you measure θ ≈ 25°, μ_s ≈ tan 25° ≈ 0.47.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. F = 30 N on m = 5 kg with μ_k = 0.4. Find a.
2. 0.2-kg ball 30 m/s rebounds at 25 m/s in 0.05 s. Find avg F.
3. 80-kg skater throws 4-kg ball at 5 m/s. Find skater's recoil.
4. Atwood: 5 kg & 3 kg, find a and T.
Compare with bench partner.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room; common slip is forgetting kinetic vs static friction in question 1.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. Action and reaction on the same body? T/F
Q2. Friction is proportional to area? T/F
Q3. μ_k vs μ_s — which is bigger?
Q4. Atwood acceleration formula?
Show on fingers.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: 1st law: no net force → no change in motion.
2nd law: F = dp/dt = ma; impulse = Δp.
3rd law: action ↔ reaction on different bodies.
Momentum conserved in isolated systems.
Friction: f_s ≤ μ_s N (static), f_k = μ_k N (kinetic), μ_k < μ_s.
slides.speaker_notes: End with the 5 takeaways. Hand out the worksheet and announce homework.
